growth_story.headline: China's income per person grew 9.3 percent a year from 1990 to 2011, then 5.8 percent from 2012 as investment paid less and housing slumped.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2011 China's income per person grew 9.3 percent a year, with a high of 13.6 percent in 2007, as productivity rose after China joined the WTO and capital built up fast. Investment climbed from 23.9 percent of GDP in 1990 to 44.1 percent in 2013, and after the 2008 global crisis growth leaned more and more on infrastructure and housing paid for with credit. Since 2012 growth has run at 5.8 percent a year, and the last decade averaged 5.4 percent against 9.0 in the decade before; the IMF links the slowdown to slower productivity growth, falling returns to investment and a shrinking workforce. The pandemic years swung from 2.1 percent in 2020 to 8.5 in 2021 and 3.1 in 2022, and a housing slump that began in 2021 has weighed on household spending since. Growth held between 5.1 and 5.5 percent from 2023 to 2025, carried more by exports than by demand at home, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Trade opening and fast capital
threads.text: Growth in the 2000s rose to 13.6 percent in 2007. The IMF links that boom to productivity gains after China joined the WTO and to a rapid build-up of capital.

citations.title: China’s Path to Sustainable and Balanced Growth (IMF Working Paper WP/24/238)
citations.quote: China’s high growth rates in the early 2000s were largely driven by increases in productivity following the WTO accession and rapid accumulation of capital

threads.title: Credit-fuelled building after 2008
threads.text: After the 2008 global crisis, growth came to rest on building infrastructure and housing, financed by fast credit growth. Private credit rose from 100.4 percent of GDP in 2008 to 149.6 percent in 2015, and investment peaked at 44.1 percent of GDP in 2013. The IMF says productivity growth slowed in the decade before the pandemic as investment went to less productive uses.

citations.title: China’s Path to Sustainable and Balanced Growth (IMF Working Paper WP/24/238)
citations.quote: Following the Global Financial Crisis (GFC), China’s growth became increasingly dependent on investment in infrastructure and housing.

citations.title: China’s Path to Sustainable and Balanced Growth (IMF Working Paper WP/24/238)
citations.quote: This was made possible by high savings and excessive credit growth (Figure 4) accompanied by sharply rising debt levels across the economy.

citations.title: China’s Path to Sustainable and Balanced Growth (IMF Working Paper WP/24/238)
citations.quote: In the decade before the pandemic, productivity growth slowed, including because of increasingly less productive investment

threads.title: The housing slump since 2021
threads.text: Home prices have fallen since mid-2021 and housing investment has roughly halved as a share of GDP. Falling home values and a soft job market have made households careful with money, so spending at home has stayed weak.

citations.title: China Economic Update (June 2026): Rebalancing Growth

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: Housing investment has fallen from a peak of 12.3 percent of GDP in 2020 to 6.1 percent in 2025

citations.title: China Economic Update (June 2026): Rebalancing Growth
citations.quote: consumer spending remained cautious due to the negative wealth effect from falling property prices and the soft labor market.

threads.title: Ageing and falling returns
threads.text: The IMF and the World Bank both expect growth to keep easing as the workforce shrinks, investment earns less and productivity grows more slowly. Investment was still 39.7 percent of GDP in 2024, down from 44.1 percent in 2013.

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: Over the medium term, growth is projected to continue decelerating due to a declining labor force, decreasing returns to investment, and slower productivity growth.

citations.title: China Economic Update (June 2026): Rebalancing Growth
citations.quote: partially offset the structural drag from demographic aging, elevated debt, and diminishing returns to capital

threads.title: Exports carry a low-price economy
threads.text: With demand at home weak, exports and state support carried growth, and income per person grew 5.1 percent in 2025. Consumer prices rose only 0.1 percent that year. The IMF says the state-led model has brought technical gains but also low returns, excess supply in some industries and rising debt.

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: Real GDP grew by 5 percent in 2025, meeting the authorities’ target, supported by robust exports and policy stimulus.

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: the growth model based on state-led investment and industrial policy support has led to technological advances and gains in international market share

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: it has also resulted in low aggregate returns, excess supply in some tradable sectors, and the build-up of debt and financial vulnerabilities.

since_last_year.text: Trade tension with the United States flared in 2025 and then eased with a one-year truce in October, while exports helped income per person grow 5.1 percent in 2025. In the second quarter of 2026 a global energy supply shock raised costs and slowed momentum, on top of the continuing housing slump.

citations.title: People’s Republic of China: 2025 Article IV Consultation—Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for the People’s Republic of China
citations.quote: After another escalation of trade tensions in September, the US and China agreed to a one-year truce in October

citations.title: China Economic Update (June 2026): Rebalancing Growth
citations.quote: Momentum softened in the second quarter, as disruptions to global energy supply raised costs and increased uncertainty.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe weak demand at home, falling home prices and prices that barely rise, yet the data show income per person growing 5.1 percent in 2025 and at its highest level ever. Part of the gap is about how growth is measured: the IMF notes that the GDP deflator kept falling, so growth after inflation looks stronger than growth in money terms.
